    Batch correction with bixverse¶

    Python port of the R vignette Batch correction with bixverse. Original authors: Grant Neilson, Gregor Lueg and Liesbeth François.

    Intro¶

    Batch effects are systematic technical differences between experimental runs that can obscure genuine biological signal in single cell data. When datasets from multiple experiments, technologies, or laboratories are combined, cells tend to group by their source rather than by cell type. Batch correction methods aim to remove these technical artefacts whilst preserving biological variation.

    bixverse provides four batch correction approaches, each with different trade-offs:

    • fastMNN (Haghverdi, et al., 2018) identifies mutual nearest neighbours across batches: pairs of cells from different batches that are each other's closest match. Correction vectors are computed from these pairs and applied to align the embeddings. It is particularly effective when cell type composition differs across batches.
    • Harmony (Korsunsky, et al., 2019) operates on PCA embeddings using iterative soft clustering with diversity penalties. It assigns cells to clusters, estimates batch effects per cluster via ridge regression, and corrects the embedding. It tends to be fast and works well across a range of scenarios. A version 2 has been released too, see Patikas, et al., 2026, with improvements that increase scalability to larger data sets and modifications to the objective functions to not overcorrect across batches when different cell types are there.
    • BBKNN (Polanski, et al., 2020) takes a fundamentally different approach. Rather than correcting an embedding, it constructs a batch-balanced k-nearest neighbour graph by building separate neighbour indices per batch. The corrected graph can then be used directly for clustering and visualisation.
    • Seurat anchors (Stuart, et al., 2019) find pairs of cells that are mutual nearest neighbours in a space shared by two batches, score them by how much of their neighbourhood they share, and use them to pull one batch onto the other. Two flavours are available. CCA builds the shared space from canonical correlations and corrects hardest, which suits batches that don't share their cell types. rPCA projects each batch into the other's PCA basis instead: cheaper, gentler, and the better default when the batches broadly match. Both need batch-aware HVGs.

    A correction has two jobs: mix the batches and keep the biology intact. Going too hard on the first ruins the second, so bixverse scores both, following the scIB benchmark (Luecken, et al., 2022).

    Batch mixing:

    • kBET: tests whether neighbourhood batch proportions match the global ones.
    • Batch ASW: silhouette width on batch labels in the embedding.
    • iLISI: effective number of batches per neighbourhood. Works on any kNN graph.
    • PCR: how much of the embedding variance batch explains, before versus after correction.

    Bio conservation, which needs cell type labels:

    • cLISI: effective number of cell types per neighbourhood. You want one.
    • Cell type ASW: silhouette width on cell type labels.
    • Graph connectivity: whether each cell type stays one connected piece of the kNN graph.

    bv.integrate.calculate_integration_metrics() runs the lot and returns one row, every column rescaled so that higher is better.

    Preparing the data¶

    Loading the batches¶

    We use two PBMC datasets (pbmc3k and pbmc4k) as a standard benchmark for batch correction. These come from the same tissue but differ in sequencing depth and cell counts, introducing a clear batch effect.

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    dir_data = bv.io.download_pbmc_batches()

tempdir_batch_cor = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()

h5ad_paths = {
    "pbmc3k": dir_data / "pbmc3k.h5ad",
    "pbmc4k": dir_data / "pbmc4k.h5ad",
}

h5_tasks = bv.io.prescan_h5ad_files(h5ad_paths)

sc = bv.io.load_multi_h5ad(
    Path(tempdir_batch_cor.name) / "batch_cor",
    h5_tasks,
    verbose=True,
)

    Quality control¶

    Before batch correction, we filter out low-quality cells using mitochondrial gene proportions and library complexity metrics. In a multi file import the additional var columns are dropped, so the gene symbols come from one of the h5ad files.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    h5_metadata = bv.io.read_h5ad_metadata(h5ad_paths["pbmc3k"])
h5_var = h5_metadata["var"]
assert isinstance(h5_var, pl.DataFrame)

var = sc.var().join(
    h5_var.select(
        pl.col("ensembl_id").alias("gene_id"),
        pl.col("symbol_tenx").alias("gene_symbol"),
    ),
    on="gene_id",
)

gs_of_interest = {
    "MT": var.filter(pl.col("gene_symbol").str.contains("^MT-"))["gene_id"].to_list(),
    "Ribo": var.filter(pl.col("gene_symbol").str.contains("^RP[SL]"))[
        "gene_id"
    ].to_list(),
}

bv.qc.gene_set_proportions(sc, gs_of_interest, streaming=False, verbose=True)

qc_df = sc.obs(cols=["cell_id", "lib_size", "nnz", "MT"])

metrics = {
    "log10_lib_size": np.log10(qc_df["lib_size"].to_numpy()),
    "log10_nnz": np.log10(qc_df["nnz"].to_numpy()),
    "MT": qc_df["MT"].to_numpy(),
}

directions: dict[str, Literal["twosided", "below", "above"]] = {
    "log10_lib_size": "twosided",
    "log10_nnz": "twosided",
    "MT": "above",
}

qc = bv.qc.run_cell_qc(
    metrics,
    sc.cells_to_keep,
    directions=directions,
    threshold=3.0,
)

# set the cells to keep
sc.add_obs(pl.DataFrame({"cell_idx": qc.cell_idx, "outlier": qc.combined}))
sc.set_cells_to_keep(qc.cell_idx[~qc.combined])

    Cell type labels¶

    The bio conservation metrics need cell types. We cluster the uncorrected data and annotate the clusters with scType (Ianevski, et al., 2022) on a handful of canonical PBMC markers, same as in the PBMC vignette. The labels are deliberately coarse: T cells stay lumped, since splitting CD4 from CD8 on uncorrected data is asking for trouble.

    One caveat: the labels come from uncorrected data, so they carry whatever the batch effect did to the clusters. Good enough to spot a method that smears cell types together, not a ground truth.

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    bv.graph.find_clusters(sc, res=1.0, name="leiden_uncorrected")

cell_markers = {
    "CD3D": "T cells",
    "CD3E": "T cells",
    "IL7R": "T cells",
    "CD8A": "T cells",
    "MS4A1": "B cells",
    "CD79A": "B cells",
    "CD14": "Monocytes",
    "LYZ": "Monocytes",
    "FCGR3A": "Monocytes",
    "GNLY": "NK",
    "NKG7": "NK",
    "FCER1A": "DC",
    "CD1C": "DC",
    "PPBP": "Platelets",
}

cell_markers_df = pl.DataFrame(
    {"gene_symbol": list(cell_markers), "cell_type": list(cell_markers.values())}
).join(var.select("gene_symbol", "gene_id"), on="gene_symbol")

marker_list = bv.annotate.prepare_cell_markers(sc, cell_markers_df)

sctype_scores = bv.annotate.calc_sc_type_scores(sc, marker_list)

obs = sc.obs(cols=["cell_idx", "leiden_uncorrected"], filtered=True)

cell_type_anno = bv.annotate.score_clusters(
    sctype_scores, obs["leiden_uncorrected"].to_numpy()
)

obs = obs.join(
    cell_type_anno.select(
        pl.col("cluster_id").alias("leiden_uncorrected"), "cell_type"
    ),
    on="leiden_uncorrected",
    how="left",
)

sc.add_obs(obs.select("cell_idx", "cell_type"))

obs["cell_type"].value_counts(sort=True)

    Comparing the different methods¶

    Let's check out the different methods and how they behave.

    Uncorrected data¶

    Before applying any correction, we can visualise the batch effect and compute baseline metrics. All t-SNEs here use the quick-and-dirty Barnes-Hut optimiser.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    bv.embed.tsne(sc, params=bv.embed.tsne_defaults().set_params(approx="qd"))  # ty: ignore[invalid-argument-type] # manifolds-rs types set_params as BaseEmbedding
    bv.embed.tsne(sc, params=bv.embed.tsne_defaults().set_params(approx="qd")) # ty: ignore[invalid-argument-type] # manifolds-rs types set_params as BaseEmbedding

    tSNE plot (tSNEs usually look prettier... It's anyway not a good way to assess batch effect correction, so at least let's make it pleasant on the eye).

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    ax = bv.pl.embedding_plot(sc, "tsne", "exp_id", label_by="exp_id", discrete=True)
ax.set_title("Before batch correction")
plt.show()
    ax = bv.pl.embedding_plot(sc, "tsne", "exp_id", label_by="exp_id", discrete=True) ax.set_title("Before batch correction") plt.show()

    The high kBET rejection rate (so a low kbet_accept) and a low ilisi confirm a substantial batch effect, and the tSNE shows clear separation by batch. pcr_comparison is null here: it compares a corrected embedding against this PCA, so the PCA has nothing to compare against.

    fastMNN¶

    fastMNN works on batch-aware HVGs and produces a corrected embedding. It identifies mutual nearest neighbours across batches to compute correction vectors. For it to work best, we need the batch-aware HVGs. We calculate these, provide them to fastMNN (which regenerates the PCA embedding based on the batch-aware HVGs) and then run the actual algorithm.

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    batch_aware_hvg = bv.pp.find_hvg_batch_aware(sc, "exp_id")

bv.integrate.fast_mnn(sc, "exp_id", batch_aware_hvg.hvg_gene_idx)

bv.graph.find_neighbours(sc, embd_to_use="mnn")

    Harmony¶

    Harmony operates on the PCA embedding directly. Leave k as None and the number of clusters is set to one per 30 cells, capped at 100. Both versions are supported and share one numerical core in Rust. They differ in the diversity penalty, the ridge regression and how the ridge penalty gets set. The intercept is never penalised in either. bv.integrate.harmony() runs v2; the original is bv.integrate.harmony_v1(). Let's start with the original:

    Version 1¶

    In [14]:
    Copied! 
    bv.integrate.harmony_v1(sc, "exp_id")

bv.graph.find_neighbours(sc, embd_to_use="harmony_v1")

    Version 2¶

    Patikas, et al., 2026 changed four things compared to v1. The last three have knobs in bv.params.HarmonyV2Params:

    • Stabilised diversity penalty, which makes the objective scale-invariant.
    • Batch pruning in the ridge regression. A batch that puts less than batch_proportion_cutoff of its cells into a cluster is dropped from that cluster's regression. A cluster left with a single batch isn't corrected, so a cell type unique to one batch doesn't get pulled towards the others.
    • Dynamic lambda. With use_dynamic_lambda=True (the default) the ridge penalty is set per cluster as alpha times the expected counts and the fixed lambda_ is ignored.
    • Theta scaling by batch size via tau. Off by default (tau=0).

    The paper's arrowhead matrix inversion for a single batch covariate is used by both versions here, so v1 gets that speed-up too. v2 also runs only 4 k-means iterations per Harmony round versus 20 in v1. Unless you need to reproduce an old v1 result, go with v2, which is why it is the default.

    Seurat CCA¶

    Seurat's anchor methods take a different route. For each pair of batches they find cells that are mutual nearest neighbours in a shared space, treat those pairs as anchors, score them by how much of their neighbourhood they share, and then apply a kernel-weighted correction that pulls the query batch onto the reference. Batches get merged in the order of their pairwise anchor counts.

    For CCA the shared space is a canonical correlation embedding computed per batch pair. Anchors also get filtered in gene space before scoring, which is CCA-only in Seurat.

    A few things differ from Seurat's reference implementation:

    • The per-gene ScaleData step is skipped. We work directly from per-cell standardised log-normalised HVG expression.
    • M = X1^T @ X2 is never materialised. The canonical correlations come from a matrix-free randomised SVD, so memory stays at O((n1 + n2) * num_cc) rather than n1 x n2. On big batch pairs that is the difference between running and not running.
    • The correction is applied to the embedding (dims x cells), not to full log-expression.
    • The effective CC rank is max(num_cc, dims), not num_cc.

    Anchor structure comes out close to identical. Like fastMNN, CCA wants batch-aware HVGs, so we reuse the ones computed above.

    Seurat rPCA¶

    rPCA runs the same anchor pipeline on a cheaper shared space. Instead of computing canonical correlations, each batch keeps its own PCA basis and the other batch's expression is projected into it. Cross-batch neighbour queries then happen in these projected bases.

    The trade-off is the usual one: rPCA is faster and corrects less aggressively, which makes it the safer choice when your batches share most of their cell types. CCA is the one to reach for when they don't. As in Seurat, no gene-space anchor filter runs here, that step is CCA-only.

    One caveat worth knowing about both anchor methods: on data that already mixes well they have nothing to gain, and the correction can nudge the batch metrics slightly in the wrong direction while still sharpening the cell type structure. Check your uncorrected metrics before reaching for them.

    BBKNN¶

    BBKNN doesn't touch the embedding. It builds a batch-balanced neighbour graph instead: neighbours_within_batch nearest neighbours from every batch, turned into UMAP-style connectivities. Here that's 10 per batch, so 20 neighbours per cell feed the connectivities. no_neighbours_to_keep only cuts the stored kNN, and the cut stays balanced: each batch keeps its nearest ceil(15 / 2) = 8, so a cell ends up with 8 from one batch and 7 from the other.

    That makes BBKNN awkward to score. kBET and iLISI read the stored kNN, which is balanced by construction, so they come out near perfect whatever the data looks like. That's the method grading its own homework, not a sign of mixing. ASW and PCR need an embedding, and BBKNN doesn't have one, so we pass embd_to_use=None and those come back null. cLISI and graph connectivity are still fair, since they only look at cell types.

    So what does the graph actually look like? Counting edges is not enough: the connectivities are weighted, and everything downstream (clustering, t-SNE, UMAP) follows the weights. Below: the cross-batch share of the stored kNN, of the graph's edges and of its total weight, plus the median distance from each cell to its nearest neighbour in its own batch and in the other one.

    In [32]:
    Copied! 
    batch = sc.obs(cols=["exp_id"], filtered=True)["exp_id"].to_numpy()

knn_idx = sc.cache.knn.indices
knn_dist = sc.cache.knn.distances
other_batch = batch[knn_idx] != batch[:, None]

conn = sc.cache.connectivities
edge_rows = np.repeat(np.arange(conn.shape[0]), np.diff(conn.indptr))
cross_edge = batch[edge_rows] != batch[conn.indices]

pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "cross_batch_share_knn": [other_batch.mean()],
        "cross_batch_share_edges": [cross_edge.mean()],
        "cross_batch_share_weight": [conn.data[cross_edge].sum() / conn.data.sum()],
        "median_nearest_same_batch": [
            np.median(np.where(other_batch, np.inf, knn_dist).min(axis=1))
        ],
        "median_nearest_other_batch": [
            np.median(np.where(other_batch, knn_dist, np.inf).min(axis=1))
        ],
    }
)
    batch = sc.obs(cols=["exp_id"], filtered=True)["exp_id"].to_numpy() knn_idx = sc.cache.knn.indices knn_dist = sc.cache.knn.distances other_batch = batch[knn_idx] != batch[:, None] conn = sc.cache.connectivities edge_rows = np.repeat(np.arange(conn.shape[0]), np.diff(conn.indptr)) cross_edge = batch[edge_rows] != batch[conn.indices] pl.DataFrame( { "cross_batch_share_knn": [other_batch.mean()], "cross_batch_share_edges": [cross_edge.mean()], "cross_batch_share_weight": [conn.data[cross_edge].sum() / conn.data.sum()], "median_nearest_same_batch": [ np.median(np.where(other_batch, np.inf, knn_dist).min(axis=1)) ], "median_nearest_other_batch": [ np.median(np.where(other_batch, knn_dist, np.inf).min(axis=1)) ], } )

    Half the edges cross batches, but they carry only a few percent of the weight. The nearest cell in the other batch sits about twice as far away as the nearest one in the cell's own batch, and the UMAP connectivities decay with distance, so the cross-batch edges end up with next to no weight. This isn't an implementation detail: the reference bbknn package behaves the same on this data. pbmc3k and pbmc4k were run on different 10x chemistries (GemCode v1 against v2), and that gap is real.

    The fair test of a graph method is clustering, so let's run Leiden on the BBKNN graph and compare its clusters against the uncorrected ones and Harmony v2. A cluster where one batch holds more than 90% of the cells counts as unmixed.

    In [33]:
    Copied! 
    bv.graph.find_clusters(sc, res=1.0, name="leiden_bbknn")

# share of a cluster's cells from one batch above which it counts as unmixed
SINGLE_BATCH_CUTOFF = 0.9


def batch_composition(cluster_col: str) -> pl.DataFrame:
    obs = sc.obs(cols=[cluster_col, "exp_id"], filtered=True)
    per_cluster = (
        obs.group_by(cluster_col, "exp_id")
        .len()
        .with_columns(share=pl.col("len") / pl.col("len").sum().over(cluster_col))
        .group_by(cluster_col)
        .agg(n_cells=pl.col("len").sum(), top_batch_share=pl.col("share").max())
    )
    unmixed = per_cluster.filter(pl.col("top_batch_share") > SINGLE_BATCH_CUTOFF)
    return pl.DataFrame(
        {
            "clustering": [cluster_col],
            "n_clusters": [per_cluster.height],
            "n_unmixed_clusters": [unmixed.height],
            "share_cells_in_unmixed": [unmixed["n_cells"].sum() / obs.height],
        }
    )


pl.concat(
    [
        batch_composition(col)
        for col in ["leiden_uncorrected", "leiden_harmony", "leiden_bbknn"]
    ]
)
    bv.graph.find_clusters(sc, res=1.0, name="leiden_bbknn") # share of a cluster's cells from one batch above which it counts as unmixed SINGLE_BATCH_CUTOFF = 0.9 def batch_composition(cluster_col: str) -> pl.DataFrame: obs = sc.obs(cols=[cluster_col, "exp_id"], filtered=True) per_cluster = ( obs.group_by(cluster_col, "exp_id") .len() .with_columns(share=pl.col("len") / pl.col("len").sum().over(cluster_col)) .group_by(cluster_col) .agg(n_cells=pl.col("len").sum(), top_batch_share=pl.col("share").max()) ) unmixed = per_cluster.filter(pl.col("top_batch_share") > SINGLE_BATCH_CUTOFF) return pl.DataFrame( { "clustering": [cluster_col], "n_clusters": [per_cluster.height], "n_unmixed_clusters": [unmixed.height], "share_cells_in_unmixed": [unmixed["n_cells"].sum() / obs.height], } ) pl.concat( [ batch_composition(col) for col in ["leiden_uncorrected", "leiden_harmony", "leiden_bbknn"] ] )

    The clusters and the t-SNE tell the same story. Leiden on the BBKNN graph still puts most cells into single-batch clusters, barely better than doing nothing, while Harmony mixes nearly all of them. The t-SNE follows the same weights and stays split by batch. On a batch effect this strong, BBKNN on its own doesn't correct much. It's built for milder effects, where the cross-batch neighbours sit close enough to keep real weight.

    Read the two panels together. A method that tops batch mixing but drops on bio conservation has merged cell types along with the batches, which is worse than doing nothing.

    Two of these tell you little on this data set. cLISI sits at 1 for every method: six coarse, well separated cell types keep their neighbourhoods pure no matter what. Batch ASW barely moves either, since two PBMC batches of the same tissue never separate much on silhouette to begin with. Both earn their keep on finer labels and nastier batch effects. On two PBMC runs, kBET, iLISI and PCR do the talking. BBKNN's row is greyed out on the batch side: its kBET and iLISI in the table above are the artefact from its section, not a win.

    There is no universally best batch correction method. Some practical guidance:

    • Harmony is a good default. It is fast, operates on the PCA embedding directly, and handles multiple batch variables simultaneously. It tends to work well when batch effects are moderate and cell type composition is broadly similar across batches. Version 2 prunes batches per cluster and sets the ridge penalty dynamically. On this data set it is not an improvement: v1 is ahead on kBET acceptance and PCR, the rest is tied, and v2 is only modestly faster (46 ms against 51 ms).
    • fastMNN is worth considering when cell type composition differs substantially across batches. The mutual nearest neighbour approach is less sensitive to this because it only aligns cells that have a plausible biological match in another batch.
    • Seurat CCA and rPCA are the anchor-based options. Like fastMNN they only align cells with a plausible match in another batch, so they hold up when cell type composition differs. They are the heaviest of the five though, and on data that already mixes well they can make the batch metrics slightly worse. rPCA is the cheaper and gentler of the two and a sensible default; go to CCA when the batches genuinely don't share their cell types.
    • BBKNN leaves the embedding alone and hands a batch-balanced graph straight to clustering. It's the lightest touch of the lot, and that cuts both ways: when the batches sit far apart, as here, the cross-batch edges carry next to no weight and the clusters stay split by batch. Judge it on clustering, not on kBET or iLISI.

    In practice, running multiple methods and looking at quantitative metrics is the most reliable approach. No single metric captures everything: kBET and PCR only see batch, cLISI and cell type ASW only see biology, and the kNN metrics can't score a method that builds the kNN to look balanced. UMAPs and tSNE assessments should be taken with a big pinch of salt, see Chari, et al. Admittedly, they do look pretty however.
